# Gram-positive cocci

> *Staphylococci and streptococci cause illnesses as different as food poisoning and heart disease
> weeks after a sore throat. That range follows from a few traits the group shares and from the
> mechanisms by which each organism causes harm.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- Sort the Gram-positive cocci by catalase, coagulase, haemolysis and Lancefield group, and state
  what each trait reveals about the organism.
- Distinguish infection, intoxication and immune-mediated damage, using the three patterns of harm
  of *Staphylococcus aureus*.
- Explain why *S. aureus* infections tend to be walled off while *Streptococcus pyogenes* infections
  spread, and how *S. pyogenes* can damage the heart after the infection has cleared.
- Explain how the capsule lets *Streptococcus pneumoniae* cause disease, and why vaccines are made
  from it.
- Name the host, setting and route that let each main organism cause disease.
- Tell *S. aureus* from *Staphylococcus epidermidis*, and *S. pyogenes* from *S. pneumoniae*, by
  laboratory traits and pattern of harm.
:::

## The group {#sec-gpc-group}

### The group in one sentence {#sec-gpc-sentence}

Gram-positive cocci are thick-walled spheres that live on the skin and mucous membranes and cause harm
mainly when they get past a barrier. Most of the six questions have one answer for the whole group;
its members differ mainly in how damage happens.

| Question | Answer for the Gram-positive cocci |
|---|---|
| What is it built from? | Thick peptidoglycan wall and no outer membrane, so no LPS; many have a capsule or surface proteins that resist phagocytes |
| How does it get energy? | Staphylococci respire or ferment; streptococci and enterococci only ferment, but tolerate oxygen |
| How does it copy itself and change? | Binary fission; exchanges genes readily, which is how toxin genes and resistance spread |
| Where does it live, and how does it spread? | Skin, nose, throat, mouth and gut of healthy people; spread by direct contact, often on hands, and by respiratory particles |
| How does damage happen? | Three patterns: **pyogenic** (pus-forming) invasion, toxins, and immune-mediated damage |
| What does it have that my cells lack? | A peptidoglycan wall, and the proteins that build it |

### Sorting the group {#sec-gpc-key}

Four laboratory traits separate the members of the group:

- **Catalase**, an enzyme that breaks down hydrogen peroxide
- **Coagulase**, an enzyme that clots plasma
- **Haemolysis**, the destruction of red blood cells, seen as a zone around colonies on blood agar
- The **Lancefield group**, a carbohydrate on the streptococcal cell wall, used to type streptococci

::: {.concept-tree}
[Sorting the Gram-positive cocci]{.tree-title}

- Catalase-positive, in clusters: staphylococci
  - Coagulase-positive: *S. aureus*
  - Coagulase-negative: *S. epidermidis* and related species
- Catalase-negative, in chains or pairs: streptococci and enterococci
  - Beta-haemolytic, typed by Lancefield group
    - Group A: *S. pyogenes*
    - Group B: *Streptococcus agalactiae*
  - Alpha-haemolytic
    - *S. pneumoniae*: lancet-shaped pairs with a capsule
    - Viridans streptococci: chains, living in the mouth
  - Non-haemolytic: *Enterococcus*
:::

On blood agar, haemolysis takes three forms:

| Haemolysis | Around the colony | What has happened to the red cells |
|---|---|---|
| Beta | A clear zone | Lysed completely by bacterial toxins |
| Alpha | A green zone | Damaged but not lysed: hydrogen peroxide from the bacteria oxidises haemoglobin to a green pigment |
| Gamma | No change | Unaffected |

Work through the key from the arrangement of the cells, and read at each branch what the trait
reveals about the organism.

<div data-island="sorting-key" data-src="/diagrams/gpc-key.yml"></div>

## Main organisms {#sec-gpc-main}

### One bacterium, three illnesses {#sec-gpc-hook}

Three people fall ill:

- A teenager develops a **furuncle** (boil): a hot, swollen, pus-filled nodule centred on a hair
  follicle.
- Forty wedding guests start vomiting two to three hours after lunch. Most are well by the next day.
- A young woman develops a high fever, a rash and **hypotension** (abnormally low blood pressure)
  severe enough to cause shock.

One organism, *S. aureus*, can cause all three, by three different mechanisms, and each follows from
how the bacterium works.

### *Staphylococcus aureus*: infection, intoxication and immune-mediated damage {#sec-gpc-aureus}

*S. aureus* lives in the nose of about one in three healthy people at any one time
[@kluytmans1997carriage]. It carries an unusually large set of virulence factors, and different
factors produce different illnesses. The factors include:

- coagulase;
- tissue-damaging enzymes;
- many toxins.

The three patterns of harm differ in what does the damage. In an infection, the bacteria multiply in
tissue. An **intoxication** is illness caused by a toxin already formed outside the body, such as in
food, without infection. In immune-mediated damage, the host's own response does most of the harm.

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Infection | Enters through a break in the skin; coagulase walls the bacteria in fibrin; neutrophils accumulate | The teenager's furuncle, or an abscess |
| Intoxication | Multiplies in food left warm and releases a heat-stable **enterotoxin**, a toxin that acts on the gut; the toxin, not the bacteria, causes the illness | The wedding guests, vomiting within hours of a meal [@argudin2010enterotoxins] |
| Immune-mediated damage | A **superantigen**, a toxin that activates a large fraction of the body's T cells at once, sets off a damaging flood of inflammation | The young woman's **toxic shock syndrome**: fever, rash and hypotension [@llewelyn2002superantigens] |

Three conditions let *S. aureus* cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | A carrier: about one in three healthy people have it in the nose | It lives on the nose and skin without harm, so people are its reservoir |
| Where (setting) | Hands, surfaces, and food left warm | It survives drying; in warm food it multiplies and makes heat-stable enterotoxin |
| How (route) | A break in the skin | Coagulase walls the bacteria in fibrin and neutrophils gather, forming an abscess |

<div data-island="microbe-profile" data-src="/diagrams/gpc-profile-s-aureus.yml"></div>

### *Streptococcus pyogenes*: tissue-damaging enzymes and delayed immune damage {#sec-gpc-pyogenes}

*S. pyogenes*, or group A streptococcus, lives on the throat and skin. Where *S. aureus* walls itself
in, *S. pyogenes* breaks tissue barriers down, and some of its most serious effects appear after the
infection has gone.

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Spread through tissue | Enzymes digest clots, DNA and the ground substance between cells | **Cellulitis**: spreading infection of the skin and the tissue beneath it |
| Toxins | Streptolysins lyse cells; superantigens act as in *S. aureus* | Scarlet fever; streptococcal toxic shock syndrome |
| Immune-mediated damage, weeks later | Antibodies against the bacterium cross-react with the host's own tissue (**molecular mimicry**) | **Rheumatic fever**, which can scar the heart valves [@carapetis2016rheumatic] |

::: {.example}
In rheumatic fever the bacteria are gone by the time the heart is damaged, so the damage comes from
the host's response alone (see [*Microbes and their
hosts*](../principles/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-drf)).
:::

Three conditions let *S. pyogenes* cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | A person who had a throat or skin infection weeks earlier | Antibodies against the bacterium cross-react with the host's own tissue, such as the heart valves |
| Where (setting) | Close contact with a person who carries it | It lives on the throat and skin of humans only, and spreads by droplets and close contact |
| How (route) | Into the throat, or through the skin into the tissue beneath | Its enzymes dissolve clots, DNA and the ground substance, so the infection spreads |

<div data-island="microbe-profile" data-src="/diagrams/gpc-profile-s-pyogenes.yml"></div>

### *Streptococcus pneumoniae*: the capsule {#sec-gpc-pneumoniae}

*S. pneumoniae* has fewer tissue-damaging enzymes and toxins. It relies on its **capsule**, a slippery
polysaccharide coat that stops phagocytes engulfing it. Many healthy young children carry it in the
nasopharynx [@weiser2018pneumococcus]. Disease begins when it reaches an adjacent space, or the blood,
and multiplies there.

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Multiplying where it does not belong | The capsule resists phagocytes; the host's inflammation fills the space | **Otitis media** (middle-ear infection), sinusitis, pneumonia |
| Invasion of the blood and meninges | The capsule protects the bacteria in the bloodstream, most effectively when host defences are weak | **Bacteraemia** (bacteria in the blood), meningitis |

Antibodies against the capsule **opsonise** the bacteria, coating them so that phagocytes can engulf
them, so pneumococcal vaccines are made from capsular polysaccharide. There are about 100 capsular
**serotypes**, variants distinguished by the chemistry of the capsule, and vaccines include the
commonest.

Three conditions let *S. pneumoniae* cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | A person with **asplenia**, absence of a functioning spleen | The spleen clears antibody-coated, encapsulated bacteria from the blood; without it, clearance fails |
| Where (setting) | The nasopharynx of a carrier, often a young child | It lives there harmlessly and spreads by respiratory droplets |
| How (route) | From the nasopharynx into the middle ear, sinuses, lung or blood | The capsule resists phagocytes, so it multiplies there and the host's inflammation fills the space |

<div data-island="microbe-profile" data-src="/diagrams/gpc-profile-s-pneumoniae.yml"></div>

## Contrast pairs {#sec-gpc-pairs}

### *S. aureus* and *S. epidermidis* {#sec-gpc-pair-staph}

*S. epidermidis* lives on everyone's skin and causes harm differently from *S. aureus*: it makes no
coagulase and few toxins, but forms biofilm on implanted devices.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-saureus-sepidermidis.yml"></div>

### *S. pyogenes* and *S. pneumoniae* {#sec-gpc-pair-strep}

The two streptococci cause harm in different ways. *S. pyogenes* damages tissue directly with enzymes
and toxins, while *S. pneumoniae* does little direct damage and causes disease by resisting phagocytes
and provoking inflammation.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-pyogenes-pneumoniae.yml"></div>

## Beyond the main organisms {#sec-gpc-beyond}

### Supporting organisms {#sec-gpc-supporting}

| Organism | Where it lives | What separates it | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| *S. epidermidis* and other coagulase-negative staphylococci | Everyone's skin | No coagulase; few toxins; forms biofilm on plastic and metal | Infects devices such as catheters and prosthetic joints; contaminates blood cultures [@otto2009epidermidis] |
| *S. agalactiae* (group B) | Gut and vagina of about one in five pregnant women [@russell2017gbs] | Beta-haemolytic, Lancefield group B | Harmless to most adults; dangerous to **neonates** (newborn infants), who meet it at birth with immature defences |
| Viridans streptococci | Mouth | Alpha-haemolytic, no large capsule | Some ferment sugar to acid that causes **dental caries**; in the blood, they can adhere to damaged heart valves and cause **infective endocarditis**, infection of the heart valves or the inner lining of the heart |
| *Enterococcus* | Gut | Tolerates bile and salt; intrinsically resistant to several drugs | Persists in hospitals; strains with acquired resistance are difficult to treat |

::: {.callout-important}
## Is *S. aureus* a hospital superbug?
Most *S. aureus* is not MRSA and is not in hospitals: it lives harmlessly in the noses of about one in
three people. **MRSA** (meticillin-resistant *S. aureus*) is *S. aureus* that has acquired a gene for
an altered version of the protein targeted by a whole family of drugs, so the drugs bind it poorly
[@lakhundi2018mrsa]. Resistance is a trait that some strains carry, and it spread because drug use
selected the bacteria that already had it (see [*How bacteria copy themselves and
change*](../principles/bacterial-genetics.qmd#sec-gen-resistance)).
:::

### Later in the course {#sec-gpc-later}

| Organism | Where it comes up again |
|---|---|
| *S. aureus* | Skin and soft-tissue, bone and joint infections; infective endocarditis; food safety; MRSA in pharmacology |
| *S. epidermidis* | Infections of devices and implants |
| *S. pyogenes* | Throat and skin infections; rheumatic heart disease in the cardiovascular block |
| *S. pneumoniae* | Otitis media, sinusitis, pneumonia and meningitis; vaccines in immunology |
| *S. agalactiae* | Neonatal infection; screening in pregnancy |
| Viridans streptococci | Dental caries; infective endocarditis |
| *Enterococcus* | Urinary and healthcare-associated infections; resistance in pharmacology |
